title: Specific Jurisdiction Reasonableness
subject: Civil Procedure
stem: A commercial bakery oven sold in Alton by Hearthline Equipment Corp. came with a heat-control module that shorted and damaged the electronic inventory system in Hannah's catering business. Hearthline is incorporated in Delaware and has its global headquarters in New York. It is a well-capitalized international restaurant-equipment company with two distribution hubs, one repair center, and 740 employees in Alton. Over four years, it has earned $86 million from Alton customers. Hannah, an Alton resident, sues Hearthline in federal court in Alton. Hearthline concedes minimum contacts but objects that defending the case in Alton would be unfair because its in-house litigation team works from New York and would have to coordinate the suit remotely.
call: Is Hearthline's fairness objection likely to defeat personal jurisdiction?

choices.A: Yes, because minimum contacts and fairness are separate requirements, and a defendant defeats jurisdiction whenever any one fairness factor favors it.
choices.B: No, because after minimum contacts are established, jurisdiction is presumed fair, and ordinary litigation inconvenience does not overcome that presumption for a large company with extensive Alton operations.
choices.C: No, because fairness is considered only when minimum contacts are close; when contacts are clear, the fairness inquiry is omitted.
choices.D: Yes, because the company's New York litigation team would face real coordination burdens defending an Alton lawsuit, satisfying the burden factor.

rightExplanation: Hearthline's objection is not enough. Once minimum contacts are established, jurisdiction is presumed reasonable. The defendant must make a compelling showing that litigating in the forum would be gravely difficult and inconvenient. Hearthline is a large company with major Alton facilities, hundreds of employees there, and substantial Alton revenue. Its complaint that New York lawyers must coordinate an Alton case is ordinary litigation inconvenience. Alton also has a strong interest in providing a forum for an Alton resident injured by a product sold there.

wrongExplanations.A: The separate fairness inquiry matters, but no single factor automatically controls it. Courts weigh the factors together, and strong contacts make the defendant's burden especially hard to carry.
wrongExplanations.C: Strong contacts do not erase the fairness inquiry. Courts still consider reasonableness; the point is that a defendant with substantial contacts rarely defeats jurisdiction on ordinary inconvenience.
wrongExplanations.D: The burden factor asks for grave difficulty, not routine logistical cost. A large company already operating heavily in Alton is not severely disadvantaged by litigating there.
